newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong, Thai shares outpace mixed Asia markets.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong, Thai shares outpace mixed Asia markets.

text.p: Hong Kong's stock market hit a 1996 high on Monday on positive economic and corporate signals while the Thai market soared nearly five percent on news of an election in November.
The two bourses were bright spots among Asian markets that were otherwise mixed.
Tokyo ended slightly up, Taiwan slightly down, and New Zealand and Manila shares plunged more than one percent.
In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng index jumped to a new 1996 high on an improved outlook for interest rates and upward revisions in corporate earnings forecasts, brokers said.
"We are getting positive economic signals and stronger than expected corporate earnings," said Amy Wong, research director at New China Hong Kong Securities Ltd.
The Hang Seng Index put on 143.04 points, or 1.22 percent, to close at 11,902.43, following through on its 123-point rise on Friday.
Monday's close was the highest since February 4, 1994, when the index closed at 12,157.57.
Thai stocks ended up 4.87 percent in active trade as investors bought stocks across the board after welcome news that a general election would be held on November 17, brokers said.
The SET index broke through the key 1,100-point resistance level before retreating and closed up 51.06 points at 1,099.01 on active 13.3 billion baht trade.
"The buying was mainly bargain hunting by speculators and was in response to the welcome election news," said one broker.
Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa dissolved parliament on Friday and set the new polls date then.
In Tokyo, stocks closed modestly higher, with trading remaining quiet on the last day of the first half of the financial year.
Brokers said the market's attention was shifting to how the key stock index would move from October 1. The 225-share Nikkei average finished up 9.38 points, or 0.04 percent, at 21.556.40.
In the biggest decline of the day, Manila shares fell sharply by 53.93 points, or 1.67 percent, to 3,169.78 points as most blue chips slipped, traders said.

"For some time, the market has been moving sideways and in the absence of good news investors got impatient. Despite a firmer Dow Jones, the market reacted negatively," said Teresa Lee, a trader at Lippo Securities.
Traders added that some blue-chip investors shifted to secondliners. Others attributed the drop to third quarter book squaring by foreign institutional investors.
The other major decliner, New Zealand's bourse, ended sharply lower on higher-than-normal turnover, which suggested the sale of part of a large portfolio, brokers said.
The NZSE-40 Capital Index ended 31.76 points or 1.43 percent down at 2,190.26 on turnover worth NZ$62 million.

In Bombay, shares ended down but off their lows after a criminal court postponed a hearing involving former prime minister P.V. Narasihma Rao until next week. The benchmark Bombay index ended down 14.22 points, or 0.44 percent, at 3240.51.

South Korean shares closed lower on worries that foreigners would not jump into the market as actively as hoped for when the foreign shareholdings ceiling is lifted to 20 percent from 18 percent on Tuesday.
The composite index ended down 3.54 points or 0.45 percent at a provisional 789.67.
In Singapore, the Straits Times Industrials Index closed up 6.11 points, or 0.28 percent, at 2,177.16. The Australian All Ordinaries index ended up 7.4 points, or 0.32 percent, at 2290.40.
Kuala Lumpur and Jakarta shares finished up slightly.
SIMEX Brent futures prices were firmer in late trading, supported by the strength of London's gas oil futures market.
November Brent last traded at $23.54 per barrel, up seven cents from London's settlement on Friday.
Hong Kong bullion ended at US$379.95/380.45 an ounce against New York's US$380.15/65 close on Friday.
The dollar was rising against the yen in late Tokyo on a slew of stop-loss buying and investor buying.
At 1010 GMT, the dollar traded at 111.38/1.41 yen and 1.5264/69 marks.
